q: What is private property in a market economy?
r: The right of individuals and firms to own and use resources
It gives people an incentive to work and invest.
w: The right of the government to seize any asset at will
The duty to share all goods equally with everyone
The rule that no one may sell what they own

q: Which feature is typical of a market economy?
r: Competition among sellers for customers
Firms compete on price and quality.
w: A single planner setting every price in advance
A ban on private businesses of any kind
Jobs assigned by birth and tradition alone

q: What is consumer sovereignty?
r: Consumers' buying choices determine what producers make
Firms that ignore buyers lose sales.
w: The government decides what consumers must buy
Producers decide what consumers may buy
Consumers must buy only domestic goods

q: What is the 'invisible hand' idea associated with Adam Smith?
r: Self-interested choices in free markets can benefit society overall
Competition guides resources to useful ends.
w: A secret government agency sets all prices
A hidden tax that businesses pay each year
A rule that businesses must give away profits

q: What is a free enterprise system?
r: A system in which businesses can operate with limited government control
Owners may start, run and close firms freely.
w: A system in which every product is free to consumers
Free refers to freedom, not zero price.
A system in which the state runs all firms
A system in which no one may earn a profit

q: Which situation shows a command economy in action?
r: A central agency decides how many cars each factory must build
Quantities are planned rather than set by markets.
w: A bakery lowers prices to attract customers
A family farm follows ancestral methods each year
A student chooses between two job offers
That is an individual market choice.

q: A common weakness of command economies is that:
r: Planners lack the price signals that show what people want
Shortages and surpluses can persist.
w: Prices rise and fall too quickly to follow
That is a feature of markets.
Too many firms compete for customers
That is a feature of markets.
That is a feature of markets.

q: A common weakness of pure market economies is that:
r: Public goods and equal access may be underprovided
Markets alone may leave some needs unmet.

q: What is a public good?
r: A good available to everyone, where one person's use does not reduce another's
National defense and street lighting are examples.
w: A good that only wealthy people can buy
A good that is sold at a store for a profit
A good that is used up by a single person

q: What is an externality?
r: A cost or benefit that affects people not involved in a transaction
Pollution is a negative externality.
w: A fee charged by a bank for services
A tax collected on imported goods
A profit earned by a business owner

q: A factory pollutes a river and nearby residents bear the cleanup costs. This is an example of:
r: A negative externality
The residents pay a cost they did not choose.
w: No benefit reaches third parties here.
The pollution is not a good.
The scenario is not about market balance.

q: A homeowner plants a beautiful garden that neighbors enjoy for free. This is an example of:
r: A positive externality
The neighbors gain a benefit they did not pay for.
w: No cost is imposed on the neighbors.
Nothing here involves trade between countries.

q: What is the free rider problem?
r: People benefit from a good without paying for it
It discourages private provision of public goods.
w: People pay more than their fair share of taxes
That is not the free rider problem.
People refuse to use public goods at all
That is not the free rider problem.
People take rides at a discount on buses

q: Why does the government provide most public goods?
r: Private firms cannot easily charge everyone who benefits
Taxes pay for goods that markets underprovide.
w: Private firms are banned from making goods
Public goods are always unprofitable by law
The reason is the free rider problem.
Citizens refuse to use goods provided privately

q: What is a fixed cost?
r: A cost that stays the same no matter how much is produced
Rent is a common example.
w: A cost that rises with every unit produced
A cost that is paid only when a product is sold
That is a variable or selling cost.
A cost that cannot be known in advance
Fixed costs are known in advance.

q: What is a variable cost?
r: A cost that changes with the amount produced
Raw materials are a common example.
w: A cost that stays the same at all output levels
A cost that is paid only once at start-up
A cost that the government pays instead
That is not a variable cost.

q: Which is an example of a fixed cost for a bakery?
r: The monthly rent for the shop
Rent is the same whether it bakes ten loaves or a thousand.
w: The flour used in each loaf
The sugar used in each pastry
The boxes used for each order

q: Which is an example of a variable cost for a bakery?
r: The flour used to make each loaf
It rises with the number of loaves.
w: The monthly rent for the shop
The loan payment for the oven

q: How is total cost calculated?
r: Fixed costs plus variable costs
Both kinds of cost are added together.

q: A shop has fixed costs of $2,000 and variable costs of $5 per unit. What is the total cost of 400 units?
w: This adds only one unit of variable cost.
This multiplies fixed costs by output.

q: How is total revenue calculated?
r: Price per unit times the number of units sold
It is the money received from sales.
w: Price per unit minus the cost per unit

q: How is profit calculated?
r: Total revenue minus total cost
Profit is what remains after all costs.

q: A store sells 300 items at $12 each. Total costs are $2,700. What is the profit?
r: $3,600 revenue minus $2,700 cost equals $900.
w: This is revenue before subtracting costs.
This is the number of items sold.

q: What is average total cost?
r: Total cost divided by the number of units produced
It shows the cost of each unit on average.
w: Total revenue divided by the price
That is not average total cost.
That is not average total cost.
The highest cost among all products
That is not average total cost.

q: What is marginal cost?
r: The extra cost of producing one more unit
Firms compare it with marginal revenue.
w: The total cost of all units produced
The cost of the first unit only

q: What is marginal revenue?
r: The extra revenue from selling one more unit
It is the added income from one more sale.
w: The total revenue from all units sold
The revenue lost from a price cut

q: A firm maximizes profit by producing until:
r: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost
Past that point each extra unit costs more than it earns.

q: What is the break-even point?
r: The level of sales where total revenue equals total cost
Profit is zero at that level.
w: The level of sales where profit is greatest
The level of output where costs are zero
The date a business first opens
That is not the break-even point.

q: Fixed costs are $6,000. Price is $20 and variable cost is $8 per unit. How many units are needed to break even?
r: 500 units
$6,000 divided by a $12 contribution margin equals 500.
w: This divides fixed costs by the price only.

q: What is the contribution margin per unit?
r: Selling price minus variable cost per unit
It shows how much each unit adds toward covering fixed costs.
w: Selling price plus variable cost per unit
Fixed cost divided by units sold
That is fixed cost per unit.

q: What is economies of scale?
r: Lower average cost per unit as production grows
Large producers can spread fixed costs.
w: Higher average cost per unit as production grows
Equal cost per unit at all output levels
A tax break for large firms
That is not economies of scale.

q: A very large firm becomes so complex that its average cost per unit begins to rise. This is called:
r: Diseconomies of scale
Coordination problems raise costs.
w: Costs fall in economies of scale.

q: What is the law of diminishing returns?
r: Adding more of one input to fixed others eventually yields smaller increases in output
Extra workers in a crowded kitchen add less.
w: Adding more inputs always increases output equally
Adding more inputs always reduces output to zero
Prices fall as more goods are sold

q: What is gross profit?
r: Sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold
It is profit before operating expenses.
w: Sales revenue minus all expenses and taxes
Sales revenue plus the cost of goods sold

q: What is net profit?
r: The income left after all expenses and taxes are subtracted
It is the bottom line.
w: The income earned before any expense is paid
The income left after subtracting only the cost of goods sold
The total value of everything the business owns

q: Revenue is $90,000, cost of goods sold is $50,000 and operating expenses are $25,000. What is operating profit?
w: This subtracts only the cost of goods sold.
This subtracts only the operating expenses.

q: What is markup?
r: The amount added to a product's cost to set its selling price
Retailers use it to cover expenses and profit.
w: The amount a store lowers a price during a sale
The tax charged on a product at checkout
The cost of shipping goods to a store

q: A retailer buys a jacket for $40 and applies a 50% markup on cost. What is the selling price?
r: $40 plus 50% of $40 equals $60.
w: This is the markup amount only.

q: What is a markdown?
r: A reduction in the selling price of a product
Stores use markdowns to clear inventory.
w: An addition to the cost of a product

q: A $80 item is marked down 25%. What is the new price?
r: 25% of $80 is $20, so $80 minus $20 equals $60.
w: This is the discount amount only.

q: What does return on investment (ROI) measure?
r: The gain from an investment relative to its cost
It is usually shown as a percent.
w: The total amount of money invested
The time it takes to earn a salary
The tax paid on an investment

q: A business invests $20,000 and earns $3,000 in profit from it. What is the ROI?
r: $3,000 divided by $20,000 equals 0.15.
w: This is not the result of the division.
ROI is a percentage, not a dollar amount.

q: What is overhead?
r: Ongoing business costs not tied directly to a specific product
Rent, utilities and insurance are overhead.
w: The cost of raw materials in each unit
The wages of workers who make the product

q: What is a direct cost?
r: A cost that can be traced to a specific product
Materials and assembly labor are examples.
w: A cost shared by the whole business
A cost paid to the government
A cost that has not yet been paid

q: What is an opportunity cost for a business choosing between two projects?
r: The profit from the project that was not chosen
It is the value of the best alternative given up.
w: The profit from the project that was chosen
That is the gain, not the cost.
The total of all costs of both projects
The tax paid on both projects

q: Project A will earn $12,000 and Project B will earn $9,000, and only one can be done. The firm picks A. What is its opportunity cost?
r: The best alternative given up is Project B.
w: That is the gain from the choice made.
That is the difference in earnings.

q: What is a sunk cost?
r: A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered
It should not affect future decisions.
w: A cost that is expected next year
A cost that varies with output
A cost that can be refunded fully

q: A company spent $50,000 on a failed product design. Which advice reflects good decision-making?
r: Ignore the $50,000 and decide using future costs and benefits
Sunk costs should not drive the next decision.
w: Keep spending because $50,000 was already invested
This is the sunk cost fallacy.
Hide the loss from the board
Double the spending to recover the loss

q: What happens to the average fixed cost per unit as output rises?
r: It falls, because fixed costs are spread over more units
Each unit carries a smaller share.
w: It rises, because more units are made
The total stays fixed, so the share shrinks.

q: What is a business?
r: An organization that provides goods or services to earn a profit
Businesses combine resources to meet needs.
w: An agency that creates laws for a country
A group that exists only to give to charity
A place where people live and work together

q: What is a sole proprietorship?
r: A business owned and run by one person
The owner keeps all profits and bears all liability.
w: A business owned by many shareholders
A business owned by two or more partners
A business owned by the government

q: What is a major advantage of a sole proprietorship?
r: It is simple and inexpensive to start
The owner has full control.
w: It has unlimited access to investor funding
The owner is protected from all business debts
It continues forever after the owner dies
It usually ends with the owner.

q: What is unlimited liability?
r: The owner is personally responsible for all business debts
Personal assets can be used to pay creditors.
w: The owner is never responsible for debts
The business may never borrow money

q: What is a partnership?
r: A business owned by two or more people who share profits and responsibilities
A partnership agreement sets the terms.
w: A business owned by one person only
A business owned by shareholders with limited liability
A business run by a union

q: What is a corporation?
r: A legal entity separate from its owners, who hold shares of stock
Shareholders have limited liability.
w: A business owned by one individual with no legal separation
A business that is part of the government
A business owned by a group that shares unlimited liability

q: What is a key advantage of a corporation?
r: Shareholders have limited liability for the company's debts
They risk only what they invested.
w: The business pays no taxes at all

q: What is a limited liability company (LLC)?
r: A business form that gives owners liability protection with flexible taxation
It blends features of corporations and partnerships.
w: A company with a limit on how many customers it can serve
A company owned by the government with limited funds
A company that cannot make a profit

q: What is a franchise?
r: A business arrangement in which a company licenses its brand and system to operators
The franchisee pays fees and royalties.
w: A tax paid by large companies
A store that sells only used goods

q: What is a nonprofit organization?
r: An organization that uses its income to pursue a mission rather than to pay owners
Many nonprofits are tax-exempt.
w: An organization that is forbidden from earning any income
An organization owned by shareholders who receive profits
An organization that is run by the government only

q: What is a cooperative?
r: A business owned and run by its members for their shared benefit
Members often share profits.
w: A business owned by a single investor
A business that competes with all members
A business that operates only at night

q: What does 'private sector' mean?
r: The part of the economy run by individuals and companies for profit
It excludes government-run activities.
w: The part of the economy run by the government
The part of the economy run by charities only
The part of the economy that is hidden

q: What does 'public sector' mean?
r: The part of the economy owned or run by governments
Public schools and the postal service are examples.
w: The part of the economy run by individual owners
The part of the economy run by foreign firms
That is not the public sector.
The part of the economy that sells stock
That is not the public sector.

q: Which type of business provides intangible products?
r: A service business such as a hair salon
Services are not physical goods.
